note: Verbatim from the Personas research page (Notion). The policy encodings predate spec decision 41 (generic ANY-of groups) and some waiting periods differ from the current 48h default used in the demo journeys.

alice.title: Alice: 3-of-5 air-gapped guardians
alice.text:
Alice routes all traffic through Tor, has not used a web2 account in years and considers Apple and Google part of the threat model. She holds a significant amount of ETH. Operational complexity is not a barrier as long as it involves no third parties.

The configuration involves nothing that needs to remain online. She generates five EOA private keys offline on an airgapped machine, writes each on paper, seals them in waterproof pouches, then distributes them across five physically separate locations. One stays at home, one goes to a family member's house in another city, one to a bank safety deposit box, one to a trusted colleague, one to a location only she knows. Three of the five must sign to meet the threshold.

No oracle and no cloud dependence. Nothing external needs to remain operational for this to work in a decade. If her city floods and the paper at home is destroyed, four keys remain across four locations and any three still meet the threshold.

Encoded in the KB policy model as a single AND clause with one method, where the N-of-M threshold lives inside GuardianMethod:

clause 0: (guardian_method[threshold=3, set={A,B,C,D,E}])   timelock 24h

Alice's health check is a periodic self-audit asking whether each location is still intact and each paper still readable, replacing an EOA with a new one if it is not.

Device-bound passkeys (a YubiKey, for example) can replace some of the EOAs within the same structure, adding hardware attestation to an otherwise paper-based setup. A backup YubiKey stored at a second location handles physical loss. The paper-only approach avoids any hardware vendor dependency, which is why it is the default here. The YubiKey variant is a valid alternative for users who prefer hardware proof over pure paper.

bob.title: Bob: 2-of-3 with distinct trust roots
bob.text:
Bob works in product at a software company and uses DeFi on weekends. He trusts iCloud and Google with his data and wants recovery to be straightforward. He has an iPhone with iCloud, has used the same Gmail address for years, owns a Ledger for his DeFi portfolio.

Methods and trust roots:
• iCloud synced passkey. Apple controls the keystore sync.
• ZK-Email on Gmail. Google as the DKIM signer, PSE as the ERC-7969 registry maintainer.
• An EOA on his Ledger, registered once as a guardian. Nothing external.

Three distinct trust roots, no two methods share one. Any two satisfy recovery and any single failure is recoverable.

Encoded in the KB policy model as three OR clauses, one per pair:

clause 0: (passkey AND ledger_guardian)     timelock 24h
clause 1: (passkey AND zk_email)            timelock 48h
clause 2: (zk_email AND ledger_guardian)    timelock 48h

Per-clause timelocks reflect the weakest leg in the pair. Clauses involving ZK-Email get longer windows because the DKIM registry is a shared external dependency.

If Bob switches to Android, the iCloud passkey still works from any Apple device logged into his account. The Ledger EOA needs no network access to remain valid. The real risk is Apple terminating his iCloud account, which removes that recovery option without warning. Health checks catch this while he still has account access to act on the warning.

carl.title: Carl: 2-of-3 with a single crypto contact
carl.text:
Carl runs a small business. His friend Sara got him into crypto last year. He has an iPhone and a MacBook and uses iCloud for everything. For anything technical, Sara is who he calls. He has no hardware wallet, no privacy-focused accounts, no crypto contacts besides her.

Methods and trust roots:
• iCloud synced passkey. Apple.
• ZK-Email on Gmail. Google and PSE.
• Sara's wallet address, registered once as a guardian. Sara controls her own keys.

The trust roots are distinct. Apple controls the passkey, Sara controls her own keys, PSE and Google back the ZK-email recovery option. No single party controls two recovery options.

Encoded in the KB policy model as three OR clauses, one per pair:

clause 0: (passkey AND sara_guardian)       timelock 24h
clause 1: (passkey AND zk_email)            timelock 48h
clause 2: (zk_email AND sara_guardian)      timelock 48h

Setup is one session with Sara. She registers her wallet address as a guardian while Carl creates the passkey on his iPhone and generates the ZK-email proof from a DKIM-signed Gmail message. Sara needs to be online only when approving an actual recovery.

If Apple terminates Carl's iCloud account, that passkey recovery option is lost without warning. If Sara loses her keys, that recovery option goes quiet. Health checks catch both while Carl still has account access to act on the warning.

diana.title: Diana: 1-of-2 starting configuration
diana.text:
Diana works at a design agency and holds a small crypto portfolio. She has an iPhone, uses iCloud for everything and has kept the same Gmail address for years. She has no hardware wallet and no one in her circle who uses crypto.

Methods and trust roots:
• iCloud synced passkey. Apple.
• ZK-Email on Gmail. Google and PSE.

With two recovery options, a 1-of-2 threshold is a good starting point. Either credential can trigger recovery on its own, which reduces the risk of permanent lockout if one fails. Moving to a 2-of-2 threshold raises the bar against unauthorized recovery but means losing either credential permanently blocks access. The 1-of-2 starting point favours availability over compromise resistance, which is the right call for a small portfolio where lockout is the larger risk.

Encoded in the KB policy model as two OR clauses, one per method:

clause 0: (passkey)                          timelock 72h
clause 1: (zk_email)                         timelock 72h

Longer timelock than Bob's pair-with-zk_email because either method satisfies recovery alone. The moment Diana acquires a hardware wallet or a trusted contact, she can enrol a third option and move to a proper 2-of-3 threshold.

Diana's health check covers both options. The wallet prompts the device to sign a test challenge for the passkey and runs a test ZK-email proof against the live account, no transaction required.

sam.title: Sam: single-option floor
sam.text:
Sam set up a wallet last month and registered the first recovery option offered, a synced passkey on iCloud. Setup took two minutes.

The configuration has one recovery option. A synced iCloud passkey is a genuine credential backed by Apple's security model and recoverable through Apple's own account recovery flows if access is lost. For a small portfolio at the start of a crypto journey, this is a workable floor.

Encoded in the KB policy model as a single AND clause with one method:

clause 0: (passkey)                          timelock 24h

The limit is exposure to a single trust root. If Apple terminates his account, no recovery path exists. As his holdings grow, adding a second independent option changes a single point of failure into a recoverable situation. Sam does not need to act immediately. The upgrade path is there when he is ready.
